tldr: The authors propose PLAT, a new framework that drives humanoid robots by providing only future keyframe poses and their arrival times, without dense frame-by-frame reference motions. By distilling dense intermediate trajectories as privileged information into a latent prior during training and refining it via latent residual reinforcement learning, PLAT successfully executes stable whole-body motions on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid even under long-horizon commands.
hero_caption: Overall framework of PLAT. Based on a pretrained dense tracking expert, privileged dense reference transitions are distilled into a latent prior via CVAE and DAgger during training. Finally, latent residual reinforcement learning optimizes keyframe tracking accuracy without destroying the learned motion prior.
overview:
While humanoid motion imitation and reinforcement learning have advanced remarkably, existing high-precision controllers fundamentally rely on dense motion tracking, requiring a target pose at every single frame. However, in practical scenarios such as high-level planning, natural language commanding, or teleoperation, humans naturally specify sparse keyframes like "reach this pose in a few seconds." Conventional pipelines that generate dense intermediate trajectories and feed them into low-level controllers are complex to design and prone to error accumulation.

To solve this, the authors formalize the task of "Sparse Timed Keyframe Motion Tracking," where a policy receives only future keyframe poses and their arrival times, autonomously interpolating and executing stable whole-body motions. The core insight is an information asymmetry: while only sparse commands are available at deployment, full dense motion data is accessible during simulation training. Treating the dense reference trajectory as "privileged information" and compressing natural intermediate body transitions into compact latent variables enables the policy to predict plausible transitions from sparse commands at test time.

This paper introduces PLAT, a three-stage framework comprising: (1) training a dense tracking expert, (2) distilling privileged latent transitions using a CVAE and DAgger, and (3) fine-tuning via latent residual PPO. Extensive evaluations in simulation and on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid confirm that PLAT tracks targets accurately without falling even over long planning horizons (up to 50 steps), achieving smoother and more physically plausible whole-body motions than baseline approaches.
contributions: Formalization of "Sparse Timed Keyframe Motion Tracking," a new task where a humanoid generates and executes whole-body motions given only sparse future keyframes and their arrival times.

Proposal of "PLAT," a three-stage learning framework that encodes dense reference trajectories as privileged information into a latent space during training and reproduces transitions from sparse observations at deployment.

Introduction of "latent residual reinforcement learning," which applies corrections in the latent space rather than the action space, preventing the learned motion prior from collapsing during RL fine-tuning.
Extensive horizon evaluations in simulation along with zero-shot deployment on a physical Unitree G1 robot, demonstrating accurate and stable real-world whole-body control.

sections.heading: Moving Beyond Frame-by-Frame Commands: The Shift to Keyframe Tracking
sections.summary: Traditional dense reference tracking restricts policies to local trajectory following, complicating integration with high-level planners. This paper formulates sparse tracking with timed keyframes and solves it via privileged latent transition learning.
sections.details:
Thanks to reinforcement learning and large-scale motion imitation, humanoid robots can now execute agile locomotion and acrobatic movements with high precision. However, these achievements largely rely on dense motion tracking, where reference poses are fed at every single timestep.

Under dense tracking, the robot focuses strictly on local tracking to match the immediate next pose, losing behavioral flexibility and long-term reasoning capabilities. In practical applications like language-directed task planning, teleoperation, or interactive motion editing, specifying sparse goals—such as "crouch down in 3 seconds" or "turn around in 5 seconds"—is far more intuitive. Current systems typically use a separate planner to convert sparse goals into dense trajectories before passing them to low-level controllers, an approach that complicates system design and accumulates errors.

### Why Is Sparse Tracking Difficult?
When provided with only a target pose and an arrival time, the robot must autonomously infer the intermediate transition while maintaining balance. This challenge grows rapidly as the planning horizon lengthens, increasing both solution multimodality (many possible trajectories reach the same pose) and the risk of falling. Training from scratch with reinforcement learning using sparse rewards leads to intractable exploration, while naive imitation via DAgger on a dense expert fails to capture the necessary intermediate transition distribution.

### The Key Idea Behind PLAT
The authors leverage an asymmetric setup: while only sparse commands arrive during physical deployment, complete ground-truth dense reference motions are available during training. By encoding these dense transitions as privileged information into a latent space, the policy learns to predict plausible transitions from sparse observations alone (privileged latent transition learning). Furthermore, by performing residual reinforcement learning directly within the latent space, the framework optimizes keyframe arrival precision without destroying the natural motion prior.

sections.heading: Dense Tracking vs. Sparse Control: What Sets PLAT Apart
sections.summary: This section reviews dense humanoid motion tracking, sparse goal control, and privileged latent representation learning. PLAT stands out by embedding temporal state transitions as privileged information rather than static environmental properties.
sections.details:
Related work can be categorized into three main areas:

### Dense Motion Tracking for Humanoids
Learning whole-body control from motion capture data has advanced rapidly. Large-scale models such as SONIC utilize substantial data and compute to achieve remarkably robust and natural tracking. However, these systems inherently require reference poses at every single frame. PLAT benefits from dense expert priors during training, but completely eliminates the need for dense inputs at deployment.

### Sparse Motion Control
Recent efforts like BFM-Zero and AnyBody focus on generating motions from sparse keyposes or end-effector targets. However, existing sparse control frameworks primarily target goal reaching or intermediate motion interpolation. They do not explicitly solve timed tracking, where the robot must precisely pass through designated poses at specified horizons while maintaining continuous dynamic balance.

### Privileged Latent Representation Learning
Compressing simulator-only privileged information (such as ground friction, external disturbances, or future environment states) into a latent space and estimating it from onboard observations is widely used in robotics. The defining difference in PLAT is that its privileged information is not an environmental or physical parameter, but the dense transition trajectory between keyframes itself. This serves as an effective generative prior for executing natural and dynamically sound transitions from sparse commands.

sections.heading: The Three-Stage PLAT Architecture: Baking Privileged Transitions into Latent Space
sections.summary: PLAT consists of three stages: (1) training a dense expert, (2) distilling latent transitions via a CVAE using privileged intermediate trajectories, and (3) fine-tuning with latent residual RL. At deployment, only sparse keyframe commands are required.
sections.details:
The complete pipeline of PLAT is summarized in Fig. F1. Following problem formulation, the system executes three training stages in sequence.

### III-A & III-B: Problem Formulation and Framework Overview
The robot's observation consists solely of the current state $s_t$, the future target keyframe $g_{t+\Delta}$, and the normalized remaining time $\tau_t = \Delta / \Delta_{\max}$ ($o_t = [s_t, g_{t+\Delta}, \tau_t]$). The policy outputs joint position targets from this sparse command, which low-level PD controllers convert into torques. No intermediate reference frames are provided at test time.

### III-C: Stage 1 - Dense Motion Prior Learning
First, a standard dense tracking expert $\pi_E(s_t, g_{t+1})$ is trained using reinforcement learning to follow one-step-ahead reference frames $g_{t+1}$. This expert masters walking, turning, and dynamic whole-body coordination, acting as a teacher whose parameters are frozen in subsequent stages.

### III-D: Stage 2 - Privileged Latent Transition Learning
This stage forms the core of PLAT. During training only, the complete sequence of intermediate goals $G_{t:t+\Delta} = \{g_t, g_{t+1}, \dots, g_{t+\Delta}\}$ is provided as privileged information. A GRU encoder compresses this sequence into a summary feature $e_t$.
- **Posterior Network ($Q_\phi$)**: Conditions on both the sparse observation feature $h_t$ and the privileged transition feature $e_t$ to sample a latent variable $z_t$ (training only).
- **Prior Network ($P_\theta$)**: Predicts the distribution of $z_t$ using only the sparse observation feature $h_t$ (used at deployment).

In addition to behavioral cloning losses matching expert actions $a_t^E$, the model minimizes the KL divergence $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}$ between the posterior and prior. To mitigate covariate shift, an online DAgger protocol gathers expert supervisory labels along rollouts generated by the student policy. Once training is complete, the privileged encoder and posterior network are discarded.

### III-E: Stage 3 - Latent Residual Reinforcement Learning
While the policy learned via DAgger excels at motion imitation, fine optimization is still required to hit sparse keyframes precisely on schedule. However, directly fine-tuning the entire policy with PPO quickly degrades the learned natural motion prior.
To resolve this, PLAT freezes the encoder, prior, and decoder, introducing a lightweight latent residual network trained via PPO that predicts a small correction $\Delta z_t$ added to the prior latent variable ($z_t = z_t^p + \alpha \Delta z_t$). Applying residuals in latent space rather than action space maximizes tracking rewards and stability while strictly preserving the underlying human-like motion distribution.

Top-right: Distilling privileged intermediate transition information (orange box) into the latent prior via DAgger. Bottom: Freezing the prior and decoder while optimizing only the latent residual network (Residual $R_\psi$) via PPO.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Robust Long-Horizon Tracking and Hardware Validation
sections.summary: PLAT outperforms baselines by a large margin on tasks with targets up to 50 steps ahead. Ablation studies validate the latent residual design, and real-world trials confirm smooth whole-body control on the Unitree G1.
sections.details:
Experiments evaluate how well the proposed method handles varying horizons and analyze the individual contribution of each component both quantitatively and qualitatively.

### IV-A: Evaluation Setup and Metrics
Testing covers five horizon settings for $\Delta$: Single ($\Delta=1$), Short (2–10), Medium (11–25), Long (26–50), and Mixed (uniformly sampled from 1–50). Primary metrics include the keyframe arrival success rate within the final 3 steps (TKS@3), timed joint position error (Timed MPJPE@3), and timed keypoint position error (Timed MPKPE@3).

### IV-B & IV-C: Baseline Comparisons and Horizon Generalization
Under the Mixed evaluation setting (Table I), PLAT achieved the highest arrival success rate (TKS@3) and the lowest joint error (Timed MPJPE@3). Scratch RL policies performed adequately on short horizons where keyframes were close, but failed to plan transitions as the horizon lengthened. Prominent dense trackers like SONIC and TWIST2 suffered severe performance drops when supplied only with sparse keyframes, as they rely heavily on dense continuous future context. In contrast, PLAT retained high stability even over Long horizons.

### IV-D: Insights from Ablation Studies
- **Impact of Privileged Latent Modeling**: Removing privileged transition learning and training a direct sparse-to-action policy via DAgger (w/o Privileged Latent) caused substantial drops in success rate and tracking accuracy, highlighting the necessity of modeling intermediate transitions explicitly in latent space.
- **RL Fine-Tuning Strategy**: Directly fine-tuning the full policy using PPO (Direct RL Fine-tune) destroyed the learned prior, leading to dramatic performance collapse. Furthermore, PLAT's latent residual formulation (Residual Latent) outperformed conventional action-space residuals (Residual Action) across all accuracy metrics.

### IV-E: Qualitative Analysis and Real-World Unitree G1 Deployment
Visual comparisons in simulation (Fig. F3) show that while SONIC exhibited sudden, unnatural, and rigid recovery motions, PLAT generated smooth, dynamically feasible footsteps between keyframes. When deployed zero-shot on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid using identical sparse command inputs, the robot smoothly transitioned across successive poses on schedule during both locomotion and expressive upper-body motions without losing balance.

captions.F3: Motion tracking comparisons in simulation and on the physical Unitree G1 robot. The top row depicts locomotion, and the bottom row illustrates dynamic upper-body motions. In contrast to SONIC's abrupt and awkward recoveries (left), PLAT (middle and right) produces smooth and well-balanced whole-body motions in both simulation and the real robot.

sections.heading: Discussion and Limitations: Open Challenges and Future Directions
sections.summary: While PLAT offers a practical control interface without dense inputs, it still requires dense reference data and expert policies during training, and extreme planning horizons pose remaining challenges.
sections.details:
Sparse timed keyframe tracking provides a promising bridge between high-level task planners and low-level whole-body control. Combining privileged latent transition learning with latent residual RL successfully addresses this challenging problem while maintaining motion quality.

### Identified Limitations
The authors highlight several open limitations:
- **Reliance on Dense Training Data**: Although the policy runs strictly on sparse commands during deployment, offline training still requires rich dense reference motions and a pretrained dense tracking expert. Applying PLAT to skills lacking dense demonstration data remains non-trivial.
- **Uncertainty Under Extreme Horizons**: Over horizons far exceeding the 50 steps evaluated here, intermediate degrees of freedom multiply significantly. In such cases, specifying a single keyframe and arrival time may introduce too much ambiguity for the latent prior to resolve reliably on its own.

Future research aims to explore more expressive sparse command interfaces and develop training methodologies that further reduce dependence on privileged dense supervision.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A Practical Bridge Between High-Level Planning and Whole-Body Control
sections.summary: PLAT leverages dense reference trajectories as privileged latent representations during training while executing whole-body humanoid motions from sparse timed keyframes at deployment. Successful physical deployment on the G1 highlights its practical impact.
sections.details:
This paper formulated "Sparse Timed Keyframe Motion Tracking" for humanoids and introduced "PLAT," a three-stage learning framework designed to solve it.

At the core of PLAT is distilling dense tracking expertise into a sparse-conditioned latent prior via privileged latent transition learning, coupled with latent residual reinforcement learning that refines goal reaching accuracy while safeguarding natural motion characteristics. This design frees the robot from needing dense trajectory inputs at every step, allowing it to transition stably and fluidly to designated poses within specified time limits.

Thorough simulation benchmarks and successful zero-shot transfer to the Unitree G1 humanoid demonstrate that PLAT serves as a robust and practical interface connecting high-level motion planning with low-level whole-body control.

takeaways: Privileged latent transition learning—exploiting dense trajectories available only during training while deploying on sparse commands—is an effective design pattern for humanoid motion interpolation.
When fine-tuning imitation-learned policies with RL, applying residuals in latent space rather than action space prevents the destructive collapse of natural motion priors.
Standard dense tracking controllers like SONIC rely heavily on continuous future frames and degrade severely when restricted to sparse keyframe commands.
limitations: High-quality dense reference motions and a well-trained dense tracking expert remain mandatory during the training stage.
Under extremely long planning horizons, the vast space of plausible transitions can lead to motion failures or underfitting when conditioned on only a single sparse keyframe.
